# 2 Maccabees Chapter 9 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 9 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_009_page_001.jpg

---

## Council Notes

**Chapter Overview:** The death of Antiochus IV Epiphanes — one of antiquity's most detailed and theologically charged death narratives. The author presents his death as explicit divine retribution, structurally parallel to Acts 12:23 (the death of Herod Agrippa). The worm-and-stench motif (vv. 5-10) echoes Isaiah 66:24. Antiochus's letter (vv. 19-27) is almost certainly a literary construction by the author, not an authentic document.

**Key Decisions:**
- "Irremediable pain in his bowels" (v. 5): retained literal — the visceral detail is theologically deliberate (see v. 6)
- "All-seeing Lord" (v. 5): EMET/LOGOS reading preserved; PNEUMA paraphrases but retains the theological point
- "Make equal to the Athenian citizens" (v. 15): retained — this is a real civic-legal concept; PNEUMA "rights as citizens of Athens" is acceptable
- "Foster brother" (v. 29): Greek *syntrophos* — literally "one raised together with"; "foster brother" is the standard rendering

**Theological Note:** The symmetry of v. 6 is the author's explicit moral framework: Antiochus tormented the bowels of others; God torments his bowels. The narrative is not merely graphic but theologically structured. Translators should not soften the parallelism.

---

**9:1** About that time, Antiochus retreated in disgrace from the regions of Persia.

**9:2** He had entered the city called Persepolis and attempted to rob the temple and to seize the city. But the populace rose up in arms to defend themselves, and Antiochus was routed by the inhabitants and forced to withdraw in humiliation.

**9:3** While he was in Ecbatana, word reached him of what had happened to Nicanor and to the forces of Timothy.

**9:4** Overcome with rage, he conceived a plan to make the Jews pay for the injury done by those who had put him to flight. He commanded his charioteer to drive without stopping until the journey was finished. But the judgment of heaven accompanied him; for he had said in his arrogance, "When I arrive there I will make Jerusalem a mass grave of Jews."

**9:5** But the all-seeing Lord, the God of Israel, struck him with a blow that was invisible and incurable. As soon as he had spoken those words, an irremediable pain seized his bowels and bitter torments of his inner parts.

**9:6** And fittingly so — for he had tormented the bowels of others with many and strange cruelties.

**9:7** Yet he did not cease from his arrogance in the slightest; rather, his pride swelled greater still. Breathing fire in his passion against the Jews, he ordered his men to press on. But he fell from his chariot as it was careering along, and was thrown violently so that every joint of his body was wrenched by the fall.

**9:8** Thus the man who in his superhuman arrogance had thought to command the waves of the sea and to weigh the high mountains on a scale was now brought low and carried on a litter — a demonstration of the power of God plain for all to see.

**9:9** And worms swarmed out of the body of this impious man, and while he was still living in anguish and pain his flesh fell away, and because of the stench the whole army found his putrefaction revolting.

**9:10** The man who a short time before had thought he could touch the stars of heaven, no one could endure to carry, so unbearable was the stench.

**9:11** Then it was that, broken in spirit, he began to come down from his great arrogance, brought to his senses under the lash of God, since he was racked with pain at every moment.

**9:12** And when he could no longer endure even his own stench, he said: "It is right to be subject to God, and a mortal must not think thoughts equal to those of God."

**9:13** And this vile man made vows to the Lord, who would show him no more mercy, as follows:

**9:14** that the holy city, toward which he had been hastening to level it to the ground and to make it a mass grave, he would declare free;

**9:15** and the Jews, whom he had resolved not even to count worthy of burial but to hand over to the birds and the wild animals, along with their infants, he would make equal to the citizens of Athens;

**9:16** and the holy sanctuary, which he had previously plundered, he would adorn with the finest offerings; and the sacred vessels he would restore multiplied many times over; and the expenses of the sacrifices he would provide from his own revenues;

**9:17** and beyond all this he would himself become a Jew and would travel through every inhabited place proclaiming the power of God.

**9:18** But since his sufferings did not let up in the slightest — for the just judgment of God had overtaken him — having despaired of his own survival, he wrote to the Jews the letter reproduced below, in the form of a supplication. It read as follows:

**9:19** "To the worthy Jewish citizens, Antiochus the king and general sends many greetings and wishes for health and welfare.

**9:20** If you and your children are well and your affairs proceed as you wish, I give very great thanks to God, my hope being in heaven.

**9:21** As for me, I lie ill in body; yet I remember with fondness the honor and goodwill you showed toward me. Returning from the regions of Persia and struck down by a troublesome illness, I judged it necessary to take thought for the common welfare of all.

**9:22** I do not despair of my condition — for I have good hope of recovering from my illness —

**9:23** but observing that my father also, whenever he led campaigns into the upper regions, appointed his successor,

**9:24** so that, if anything unforeseen occurred or any difficult report came, those throughout the land, knowing to whom the government had been left, would not be thrown into confusion,

**9:25** and noting besides that the neighboring princes, the neighbors of my kingdom, are watching for opportunities — I have appointed my son Antiochus as king, whom I have often entrusted to most of you when I was traveling at speed to the upper provinces. I have written to him what I set down below.

**9:26** I therefore urge and beg you to remember the public and private benefits you have received and to maintain each of you your goodwill toward me and my son.

**9:27** For I am convinced that he will deal with you with gentleness and kindness, following my policy of goodwill toward you."

**9:28** So the murderer and blasphemer, having endured the most terrible sufferings — such as he had inflicted on others — met his end in a most miserable fashion among the mountains in a foreign land.

**9:29** Philip, his foster brother, conveyed the body home; but then, fearing the son of Antiochus, he withdrew to Ptolemy Philometor in Egypt.
